set.detail:
In spring 211, unable to break the Roman siege of Capua, Hannibal took a picked force of perhaps 30,000 men, left his camp fires burning, and marched on Rome by the Via Latina, devastating the land of Sidicini, Cales, the Volsci and Latium, crossing the Anio, and camping eight kilometres from the city, near the third milestone of the Via Nomentana. He hoped that the threat would force the Roman armies at Capua to withdraw, or perhaps that Rome would collapse. With 2,000 cavalry he rode up to the Colline Gate and around the walls by the temple of Hercules.

Rome did not panic as Hannibal hoped. Fulvius Flaccus, warned of the march, followed him with 15,000 picked men, while the consuls Gnaeus Fulvius Centumalus and Publius Sulpicius Galba had their new legions in Rome. The two armies drew up before the walls on two successive days, but storms broke out each time, and Hannibal did not attack. Livy (26.11) tells two famous anecdotes: that the land on which Hannibal was camped was sold at auction in Rome for its full price, and that Hannibal, in revenge, auctioned the banking shops around the Forum. Livy also says that reinforcements were being sent to Spain at that very moment. Hannibal withdrew, raided the sanctuary of Feronia at Lucus Feroniae, and returned to the south.

Polybius (9.5-9) provides an account of the march that differs from Livy's in route and detail, and praises the courage of both sides. The march was a failure: the siege of Capua continued, and Capua fell soon afterwards. Hannibal ad portas ('Hannibal at the gates') became a proverbial expression of mortal danger, used by Cicero and later by others. Modern historians debate whether Hannibal ever seriously considered taking Rome, which he lacked the siege equipment for, or whether the march was purely a diversionary manoeuvre. The march also shows how Rome's manpower reserve allowed it to defend the capital and maintain several armies in the field simultaneously.

scholarship: Lazenby, Hannibal's War (1978)
Seibert, Hannibal (1993)

set.detail:
By 211 the Scipio brothers had pushed the Roman front in Spain far south of the Ebro, recapturing Saguntum, and had hired some 20,000 Celtiberian mercenaries. Facing three Carthaginian armies, under Hasdrubal Barca, Mago Barca and Hasdrubal son of Gisco, they decided to divide their forces: Publius with two-thirds of the Roman and allied troops would attack Mago and Hasdrubal son of Gisco near Castulo, while Gnaeus, with one-third and the Celtiberians, would attack Hasdrubal Barca near Amtorgis (or Ilorci).

The plan failed. Hasdrubal Barca bribed the Celtiberians to go home. Publius, harassed by the Numidian cavalry of the young Masinissa, tried to intercept the Ilergetan chief Indibilis, who was coming with 7,500 men to join the Carthaginians. He was surrounded by the Carthaginian armies and killed with most of his army. Gnaeus, learning of his brother's defeat and abandoned by his mercenaries, retreated, was caught by the combined Carthaginian forces on a hill, built a makeshift rampart of saddles and baggage, and was killed in the assault, 29 days after his brother. Livy (25.32-36) places the battles in the upper Baetis valley; Pliny says Gnaeus died at Ilorci (perhaps Lorca).

The survivors, perhaps 9,000 men, retreated north of the Ebro, where an equestrian officer, Lucius Marcius Septimus, rallied them and held the line until Claudius Nero arrived later in 211. The disaster nearly cost Rome Spain, but the Carthaginians failed to exploit it, divided by quarrels among their generals and by Spanish tribal politics. It also gave the 25-year-old son of Publius, Publius Cornelius Scipio, the chance to be elected to the Spanish command in 210 with a desire for revenge. Historians judge the Scipios' strategic division a serious error, compounded by their dependence on unreliable mercenaries, but they had held Spain for seven years and prevented reinforcements from reaching Hannibal.

scholarship: Richardson, Hispaniae (1986)
Lazenby, Hannibal's War (1978)

set.detail:
During the Second Punic War, at the height of the financial crisis, Rome reformed its monetary system. The silver denarius, marked X (ten asses) and showing the helmeted head of Roma and the Dioscuri on horseback with the legend ROMA, was introduced together with the quinarius (V, five asses) and the sestertius (IIS, two and a half asses), as well as a new gold coinage and a reduced bronze coinage based on the sextantal as of about 55 grams. The victoriatus, a silver coin of about three-quarters of a denarius showing Victory crowning a trophy, was struck alongside it, mainly for use in southern Italy and with Greek trading partners.

The date of 211, now generally accepted, was established by Mattingly and Robinson in the 1930s and confirmed by archaeological evidence: the excavations at Morgantina in Sicily, destroyed by the Romans in 211, revealed early denarii in a context sealed by that destruction (Buttrey). Pliny (33.44) gives a date of 269 for the first Roman silver coinage, which probably refers to the earlier didrachms. The denarius originally weighed 4.5 grams, or 1/72 of a Roman pound, and was reduced to 3.9 grams (1/84 pound) by about 200, a standard it kept until Nero.

The reform replaced the debased quadrigatus coinage and created a coherent system of silver, gold and bronze. It was struck at multiple mints in Italy and Sicily during the war, and the denarius became the basic coin of the Roman world for 450 years. Crawford's Roman Republican Coinage (RRC 44 onwards) catalogues the early issues. The reform is a measure of the Republic's capacity for innovation under pressure, and of its access to silver, increasingly from Spain after Scipio's conquests. Its introduction also marks the shift of the Roman economy towards silver coinage, which accelerated with the spoils of the eastern wars in the second century. The tariff of ten asses to the denarius changed to sixteen around 141.

scholarship: Crawford, Roman Republican Coinage (1974)
Buttrey, The Morgantina Excavations and the Date of the Roman Denarius (1965)
Mattingly and Robinson, The Date of the Roman Denarius, PBA 18 (1932)

set.detail:
In 211 the praetor Marcus Valerius Laevinus, commanding the Roman fleet in the Adriatic, attended an assembly of the Aetolian League and persuaded the Aetolians to join the war against Philip V. Livy (26.24) summarises the treaty: the Aetolians would make war on Philip by land, Rome would support them with at least 25 quinqueremes; the territory and towns captured between Aetolia and Corcyra would go to the Aetolians, while the Romans would take the movable property, including the people; neither party would make a separate peace with Philip. The treaty was open to Elis, Sparta, Attalus I of Pergamon, and the Illyrian kings Pleuratus and Scerdilaidas.

A partial Greek copy of the treaty, found at Thyrrheion in Acarnania in 1949, confirms Livy's version and adds details. It shows that the treaty provided that if Rome and the Aetolians jointly captured a city, the Aetolians would keep the city and its land and the Romans the movables; if a city surrendered, it could join the Aetolian League. The inscription is important evidence for Roman diplomatic practice, the earliest original document of a Roman treaty in the Greek East.

The treaty showed Rome's willingness to wage war through allies and its brutality: the sack of Anticyra, Aegina and Oreus, with the enslavement of their populations, shocked Greek opinion, and Rhodian, Egyptian and Athenian diplomats tried to mediate. Polybius (9.37-39, 11.5-6) preserves speeches denouncing the Aetolians for bringing 'barbarians' into Greece. When Rome sent no troops after 208, the Aetolians, exhausted, made a separate peace with Philip in 206, which Rome regarded as a breach and used as a reason to refuse Aetolian requests in 200. Historians (Badian, Eckstein) see the treaty as an example of the limited aims of Roman policy in the East at that time: keeping Philip busy without committing major resources.

scholarship: Badian, Aetolica, Latomus 17 (1958)
Eckstein, Rome Enters the Greek East (2008)
Klaffenbach, Der römisch-ätolische Bündnisvertrag (1954)

set.detail:
After the death of his father and uncle in 211, the Roman position in Spain was held by Lucius Marcius and then by Gaius Claudius Nero, who achieved little. In 210, Livy (26.18-19) says, the Senate decided to send a proconsul and asked the people to elect one; when no experienced candidate came forward, Publius Cornelius Scipio, aged about 25, who had held only the aedileship (213), stood and was elected unanimously by the centuries. It was the first time a private citizen who had not held the consulship or praetorship received consular imperium by popular vote, a precedent that would be invoked for Pompey.

Livy surrounds the election with the elements of the Scipio legend: the young man's piety, his daily visits to the Capitol to commune with Jupiter, the rumours that he was the son of a god who had visited his mother in the form of a snake, and the charisma that he cultivated. Polybius (10.2-5), who knew Scipio's friend Laelius, rejects divine inspiration and insists that Scipio was a rational calculator who exploited belief in his divine favour to inspire his men. He recounts how Scipio won the aedileship by standing alongside his brother Lucius, and earlier saved his father's life at the Ticinus at the age of 17.

Scipio landed at Emporiae in late 210 with 10,000 infantry and 1,000 cavalry, accompanied by the propraetor Marcus Junius Silanus, and wintered at Tarraco, gathering intelligence on the three Carthaginian armies, which were far apart. His appointment was the beginning of the career that ended the war. Modern scholars (Scullard, Hoyos) see the election as the result of political manoeuvring by the Cornelii and their allies, and of a broader willingness to break constitutional norms under the pressures of war, as with the repeated consulships of Fabius and Marcellus. The command was prorogued annually until 206, giving Scipio an unusually long tenure in which to form a professional army loyal to him, a development with long-term implications for the Republic.

scholarship: Scullard, Scipio Africanus: Soldier and Politician (1970)
Hoyos, Hannibal's Dynasty (2003)

set.detail:
In spring 209, while the three Carthaginian armies were dispersed in central and southern Spain, each at least ten days' march from New Carthage, Scipio marched from the Ebro with about 25,000 infantry and 2,500 cavalry, while Laelius took the fleet along the coast. Polybius (10.6-20) says the march took seven days, which seems impossible for the 450 kilometres; some suggest a start further south. The city, on a peninsula with a lagoon to the north and the harbour to the south, was defended by only 1,000 soldiers and armed citizens under Mago (not Barca).

Scipio had learned from fishermen of Tarraco that the lagoon could be forded at low tide, or when a north wind drove the water out, in the afternoon. After an assault on the isthmus gate and the walls failed in the morning, Scipio renewed it in the afternoon and sent 500 men across the lagoon, wading waist-deep, at the moment the water receded. Scipio told his soldiers that Neptune had promised him help. The party scaled the undefended walls, and the city fell. Polybius describes the Roman custom of killing every living thing, even dogs, after storming, until the signal for plunder.

The capture of New Carthage was the most important single success of the war in Spain. Scipio took the Carthaginian treasury, 18 warships, large supplies of grain and arms, and 300 Spanish hostages, whom he treated generously, sending them home to win over their peoples. He freed the 10,000 citizens and enrolled 2,000 artisans as public slaves, promising freedom at the end of the war. Livy (26.50) adds the story of the 'continence of Scipio', who returned a beautiful captive to her fiancé Allucius. Modern debate concerns the lagoon phenomenon (tide or wind) and Polybius' reliance on Laelius and on Scipio's letter to Philip V. The capture provided Scipio with a base, the silver mines of the region and a reputation for divine favour, and it became the model of a bold strategic strike.

scholarship: Scullard, Scipio Africanus (1970)
Lazenby, Hannibal's War (1978)
Walbank, A Historical Commentary on Polybius II (1967)

set.detail:
In 208, Hasdrubal Barca was preparing to march to Italy when Scipio found his army of about 25,000 camped on a plateau near Baecula, in the upper Guadalquivir valley near Castulo, with a river at its rear and terraced slopes in front. Polybius (10.38-40) describes the position: a first terrace with light troops and a higher terrace with the main camp. Scipio, with about 35,000 men, sent his light troops to attack the first terrace, then took the main body in two columns, under himself and Laelius, up the flanks of the hill to attack Hasdrubal's main force as it was forming up.

The attack succeeded: the Carthaginian army was defeated with heavy losses (8,000 killed, according to Polybius; Livy gives 8,000 dead and 12,000 prisoners). But Hasdrubal, who had expected defeat and had already sent his elephants and treasury ahead, withdrew with most of his Carthaginian troops and marched north-west towards the Tagus, then crossed the Pyrenees by the west and reached Gaul, where he spent the winter recruiting. Scipio did not pursue, fearing the other two Carthaginian armies. After the battle, the Spanish acclaimed Scipio as king, which he refused, preferring the title imperator, as Polybius notes.

Modern opinion of Baecula is divided. Polybius praises the tactical skill of the double flank attack, a manoeuvre Scipio would develop at Ilipa, and the battle shows the Roman army's increasing flexibility under a single commander. But Hasdrubal achieved his strategic aim: he escaped with an army to Italy, where he was defeated at the Metaurus only by the brilliant march of Claudius Nero. Critics in Rome, including Fabius, accused Scipio of allowing Hasdrubal to escape. Archaeological surveys at Cerro de las Albahacas near Santo Tomé (Jaén) since 2001 have identified the battlefield with sling bullets, nails and weapons, confirming the site's location.

scholarship: Bellón et al., Baecula: arqueología de una batalla (2015)
Lazenby, Hannibal's War (1978)

set.detail:
In spring 207 Hasdrubal Barca crossed the Alps with about 30,000 men, faster than his brother had, recruited Gauls and Ligurians, besieged Placentia in vain, and marched down the Adriatic coast towards Umbria. Rome had six legions in the north under the consul Marcus Livius Salinator and the praetor Lucius Porcius Licinus; the other consul, Gaius Claudius Nero, faced Hannibal in Apulia. Hasdrubal sent messengers to Hannibal proposing a meeting in Umbria; they were captured by Roman foragers near Tarentum, and their letters brought to Nero.

Nero then took the boldest decision of the war: leaving most of his army to watch Hannibal, he marched north with 6,000 infantry and 1,000 cavalry, covering about 400 kilometres in perhaps a week, with food supplied by the towns along the route. He entered Livius' camp near Sena Gallica at night so that Hasdrubal would not notice. Hasdrubal, however, heard the trumpet signalling two consuls and decided to retreat across the Metaurus by night; his guides deserted, and his army was caught on the banks of the river. In the battle, Hasdrubal's Spaniards and Ligurians held against Livius, the Gauls were on a hill against Nero, who then led part of his force behind the Roman line and attacked the Spanish flank and rear. Hasdrubal's army was destroyed and he died charging into a Roman cohort.

Polybius (11.1-3) says that 10,000 Carthaginians and Gauls were killed against 2,000 Romans; Livy gives 56,000 and 8,000, figures far too high. Nero returned to Apulia and threw Hasdrubal's head in front of Hannibal's camp; Hannibal is said to have recognised the fate of Carthage. Livy's version of the march (27.43-51) became a Roman epic of patriotism, and Horace wrote that the Metaurus restored Roman fortune. The battle ended any chance that Hannibal would be reinforced from Spain, and he withdrew to Bruttium. The exact battlefield on the Metaurus, near Fossombrone or near the coast, remains disputed.

scholarship: Lazenby, Hannibal's War (1978)
Goldsworthy, The Punic Wars (2000)

set.detail:
In 206 Carthage made a final effort in Spain, assembling under Hasdrubal son of Gisco and Mago Barca, Polybius says, 70,000 infantry, 4,000 cavalry and 32 elephants (Livy: 50,000 and 4,500) near Ilipa (Alcalá del Río, north of Seville). Scipio had about 45,000 infantry and 3,000 cavalry, of whom almost half were Spanish allies of doubtful reliability. For several days both armies deployed late in the day in the same formation: Romans in the centre, Spaniards on the wings for Scipio; Africans in the centre, Spaniards on the wings for Hasdrubal, and returned to camp without fighting.

On the day of battle Scipio fed his men at dawn and attacked early, catching the Carthaginians unfed and hastily formed in their usual order. He reversed his own deployment: the legions were on the wings, the Spaniards in the centre. The Roman wings advanced, then turned in columns towards the enemy wings, wheeling into line in a complex manoeuvre described by Polybius (11.20-24), while the Spanish centre advanced slowly, pinning the Carthaginian Africans without engaging. The Carthaginian Spaniards on the wings were crushed; the elephants panicked. The Africans in the centre, hungry and tired after hours in the sun, retreated; a storm interrupted the pursuit. Hasdrubal escaped to Gades with a few thousand men.

Ilipa ended Carthaginian rule in Spain. Hasdrubal fled to Africa, Mago held Gades for a few months before leaving for the Balearics and Italy, and the Spanish peoples went over to Rome. Polybius regarded the battle as Scipio's masterpiece; modern military historians rank it among the finest examples of ancient generalship, showing the Roman manipular army's tactical flexibility under a commander who had trained it for years. Some (Lazenby) express doubts about the details of Polybius' description of the manoeuvre. Scipio settled his veterans in Italica, met Syphax in Africa, received Masinissa's defection, and returned to Rome to stand for the consulship of 205 with the plan of invading Africa.

scholarship: Scullard, Scipio Africanus (1970)
Lazenby, Hannibal's War (1978)

set.detail:
After the Aetolian League made a separate peace with Philip V in 206, Rome sent the proconsul Publius Sempronius Tuditanus with 10,000 infantry, 1,000 cavalry and 35 ships to Epirus in 205. The Epirotes mediated, and peace was concluded at Phoenice, the main city of the Chaonians. Livy (29.12) gives the terms: Rome kept the Parthini, Dimale, Bargullum and Eugenium, while Philip received the Atintani, subject to the Senate's approval. The treaty listed as adherents on Philip's side Prusias of Bithynia, the Achaeans, the Boeotians, the Thessalians, the Acarnanians and the Epirotes; on Rome's side, the Ilians, Attalus I, Pleuratus, Nabis of Sparta, the Eleans, the Messenians and the Athenians.

The treaty ended the First Macedonian War, which had been inconclusive: Rome had fought with few troops of its own, relying on Aetolia and Attalus, and its aim, to prevent Philip from helping Hannibal, had been achieved. For Philip, Phoenice was a moderate success: he had gained the Atintani and part of Illyria, and his position in Greece was intact. The list of adherents is controversial: many historians think that the names of Ilium and Athens were added later by the Roman annalistic tradition to justify the war of 200 on the grounds that Philip had attacked Roman allies.

The peace of Phoenice allowed Rome to concentrate on Africa, where Scipio landed in 204, and Philip to turn eastwards, where he expanded his power in the Aegean in the following years. Historians (Holleaux, Badian, Gruen) see Phoenice as the end of the first phase of Roman involvement in Greece, in which Rome had no wish for territorial expansion, and debate whether the Romans considered the treaty a mere truce. The question of whether Rome had 'friends' in the Greek world that it was obliged to defend, raised in the list of adherents, became the legal pretext for the Second Macedonian War, declared only five years later.

scholarship: Holleaux, Rome, la Grèce et les monarchies hellénistiques (1921)
Gruen, The Hellenistic World and the Coming of Rome (1984)
Eckstein, Rome Enters the Greek East (2008)

set.detail:
In 205, after frequent showers of stones, the decemviri consulted the Sibylline Books and found an oracle that whenever a foreign enemy invaded Italy, he could be expelled if the Idaean Mother were brought from Pessinus to Rome. The Delphic oracle, consulted by the envoys bringing gifts from the Metaurus spoils, confirmed the instruction and told them to seek the help of Attalus I. A Roman embassy of five, led by Marcus Valerius Laevinus, went to Pergamon, where Attalus received them and took them to Pessinus (or, some think, to Mount Ida in the Troad), where they received the sacred black stone that embodied the goddess.

The ship arrived at Ostia in April 204. The Senate ruled that the best man in Rome should receive her; Publius Cornelius Scipio Nasica, son of Gnaeus Scipio Calvus, still a young man, was chosen. The matrons, among them Claudia Quinta, passed the stone hand to hand to the city, where it was placed in the temple of Victory on the Palatine on 4 April, while the people offered incense and gifts and a lectisternium was held. The Ludi Megalenses were instituted, and a temple was begun on the Palatine, dedicated in 191. Later legend, recorded by Ovid, tells how the ship ran aground in the Tiber and Claudia Quinta, accused of unchastity, freed it by pulling it with her girdle.

The introduction of the cult was a calculated act of state religion at a critical moment of the war, a year before Scipio's invasion of Africa and two before Hannibal's departure. It strengthened ties with Pergamon and the Trojan legend, since the Magna Mater came from the region of Troy, supporting the claim of Roman descent from Aeneas. The orgiastic aspects of the cult, with its eunuch priests (galli) from Phrygia, were restricted: Roman citizens were forbidden to serve as galli until the time of Claudius. Modern scholars (Gruen, Burton) have seen in the episode a combination of diplomatic, religious and political motives, including rivalry among Roman aristocratic families, while excavations on the Palatine have identified the temple's podium and Phrygian votive figurines.

scholarship: Gruen, Studies in Greek Culture and Roman Policy (1990)
Burton, The Summoning of the Magna Mater to Rome, Historia 45 (1996)
Roller, In Search of God the Mother (1999)

set.detail:
In 205 Scipio, consul, received Sicily as his province with permission to cross to Africa if he thought it in the public interest. The Senate, influenced by Fabius, gave him only the two legions of Cannae survivors in Sicily, which he supplemented with 7,000 volunteers and the materials provided by the Etruscan and Umbrian cities. He spent 205 training his army and recovered Locri, where his legate Pleminius committed sacrilege; a senatorial commission visited Sicily in 204, inspected his army and fleet, and authorised the expedition.

In spring 204 Scipio sailed from Lilybaeum with perhaps 25,000 to 35,000 men (Livy records estimates from 10,000 infantry and 2,200 cavalry to 35,000 men) in 400 transports escorted by 40 warships, and landed near the Promontory of Apollo (Cape Farina), near Utica. He was joined by Masinissa, who arrived with a few hundred horsemen after losing his kingdom to Syphax. Scipio defeated the Carthaginian cavalry at Salaeca, ravaged the country, took 8,000 prisoners, and besieged Utica, but was forced to raise the siege by the arrival of Hasdrubal son of Gisco and Syphax, who had married Hasdrubal's daughter Sophonisba, with large armies. He wintered on a promontory near Utica, the Castra Cornelia, supplied from Sicily and Sardinia.

The landing was the decisive strategic stroke of the war: it brought the war home to Carthage and forced the recall of Hannibal. Fabius had argued in the Senate debate that Scipio should first defeat Hannibal in Italy, and that an African invasion risked repeating Regulus' disaster; Scipio argued that only an attack on Carthage would force Hannibal to leave. Livy (28.40-45) gives the speeches. Historians see the debate as reflecting both strategic and political rivalries, Fabius' faction being wary of the popularity of the young general. The Castra Cornelia remained a recognised place name in Caesar's day.

scholarship: Scullard, Scipio Africanus (1970)
Lazenby, Hannibal's War (1978)

set.detail:
In winter 204/3, the armies of Syphax (Polybius: 50,000 infantry and 10,000 cavalry) and Hasdrubal son of Gisco (30,000 and 3,000) camped about 1.5 kilometres apart near Utica, the Numidians in huts of reeds and branches, the Carthaginians in huts of timber and earth. Syphax proposed a peace in which Hannibal would leave Italy and Scipio Africa. Scipio pretended to negotiate and sent soldiers disguised as slaves with his envoys to spy on the layout of the camps.

In spring 203, after breaking off the negotiations, Scipio attacked at night. Laelius and Masinissa set fire to the Numidian camp; the Numidians, thinking the fire was accidental, rushed out unarmed and were cut down. The Carthaginians, seeing the fire, came to help and were attacked as Scipio set their camp on fire too. Polybius (14.4-5) describes the scene as the most terrible spectacle he had heard of; Livy (30.5-6) says 40,000 were killed or burned and 5,000 captured. Hasdrubal and Syphax escaped.

The burning of the camps was a coup that broke the military power of Carthage and Syphax at a stroke. It is also controversial, since Scipio used the pretext of negotiations to gather intelligence, an act that Polybius treats as clever stratagem and some Roman writers as a breach of good faith. The victory forced Carthage to raise a new army, which Scipio defeated at the Great Plains a few weeks later, and led to the capture of Syphax by Laelius and Masinissa, the fall of Cirta and the tragic death of Sophonisba. Carthage then recalled Hannibal and Mago and opened peace negotiations. Polybius admired Scipio's combination of deception and decisive action as the mark of a great commander, while modern historians debate how much the episode was improved in the Scipionic tradition.

scholarship: Scullard, Scipio Africanus (1970)
Goldsworthy, The Punic Wars (2000)

set.detail:
After the burning of the camps and the defeat at the Great Plains, the Carthaginian senate sent envoys to Scipio to negotiate and recalled Hannibal from Bruttium and Mago from Liguria. Livy (30.20) describes Hannibal's response: he gnashed his teeth and groaned, saying that he had been recalled not by the Roman people, whom he had defeated so often, but by the envy of the Carthaginian senate. He embarked from Croton in autumn 203, after sixteen years in Italy, with perhaps 15,000 to 20,000 veterans.

Livy also reports that Hannibal killed Italian soldiers who refused to follow him to Africa in the temple of Juno Lacinia, a story many historians consider Roman propaganda (it is told differently by Diodorus and Appian). Before leaving he set up a bilingual inscription in the same temple, which Polybius later read, recording his deeds. Mago, wounded in the thigh in a battle against the Romans in Insubria, died at sea on the way home. Hannibal landed at Leptis Minor, in the Byzacium, and wintered at Hadrumetum, recruiting Numidians and Moors and gathering elephants.

The preliminary peace negotiated with Scipio in late 203 provided for the evacuation of Italy, the surrender of the fleet except 20 ships, a payment of 5,000 talents and the recognition of Masinissa. It was accepted by Carthage and sent to Rome, where the Senate and people ratified it. But in early 202, while Carthaginian envoys were in Rome, the Carthaginians seized Roman supply ships driven ashore by a storm, and attacked the envoys Scipio sent to protest. The truce broke down, and the war resumed. Hannibal's departure ended the war in Italy; his long presence had devastated large parts of the south, and Roman reprisals against his allies continued for years. Modern historians debate whether the recall was a mistake, since Hannibal could still have tied down Roman armies in Bruttium.

scholarship: Lancel, Hannibal (1998)
Hoyos, Hannibal: Rome's Greatest Enemy (2008)

set.detail:
In autumn 202 (the date is debated; some prefer October), Hannibal and Scipio met near Zama, south-west of Carthage. Polybius (15.5-8) and Livy describe an interview between the two generals before the battle, which Polybius took from Laelius. The site is debated: Polybius names Margaron (perhaps Naraggara, near Sakiet Sidi Youssef), Livy Naraggara, and Nepos and later sources Zama. Hannibal had 80 elephants, 12,000 mercenaries (Ligurians, Celts, Balearic slingers, Moors), a second line of Carthaginian and Libyan levies, and his veterans of Italy in the third line, about 36,000 infantry in all, and 4,000 cavalry. Scipio had about 29,000 infantry and 6,000 cavalry, including 4,000 Numidian horse under Masinissa.

Scipio arranged his maniples in columns, with lanes between them filled by light troops, through which the elephants could be channelled. Trumpets and horns frightened the elephants, many of which ran through the lanes or stampeded onto their own cavalry, which Laelius and Masinissa then routed and pursued. The Roman hastati broke the mercenaries, who fell back on the second line, which refused to admit them; the two lines fought each other. Scipio then reformed his line, moving the principes and triarii to the wings, and engaged Hannibal's veterans in a long, hard struggle. The return of Laelius and Masinissa's cavalry against the rear of the Carthaginian army decided the battle.

Polybius says that 20,000 Carthaginians were killed and the same number captured; the Romans lost 1,500 (Livy: 2,000). Hannibal escaped to Hadrumetum and advised Carthage to make peace. Zama ended the Second Punic War and established Rome as the dominant power in the western Mediterranean. Scipio received the cognomen Africanus. The battle is considered a model of the use of reserves and of combined arms. Modern historians note that Scipio's superiority in cavalry, thanks to Masinissa, was decisive, reversing the situation at Cannae, and that Hannibal's tactical plan, with its three lines, was sound but hampered by the quality of his troops.

scholarship: Scullard, Scipio Africanus (1970)
Lazenby, Hannibal's War (1978)
Goldsworthy, The Punic Wars (2000)

set.detail:
After Zama, Carthage sent envoys to Scipio, who imposed terms ratified by the Roman Senate and people in 201. Polybius (15.18) gives them: Carthage kept its territory in Africa as it had been before the war, within the 'Phoenician trenches' (fossae Phoeniciae), with its own laws and without a garrison; it returned all prisoners and deserters; surrendered all warships except ten triremes and all elephants, and agreed to train no more; it could make no war outside Africa, and inside Africa only with Roman permission; it restored to Masinissa all the land that had belonged to him or his ancestors; it supplied the Roman army with grain and pay for three months; it paid 10,000 talents over fifty years; and it gave 100 hostages chosen by Scipio, aged between 14 and 30.

Hannibal, who silenced a senator opposing the terms, persuaded the Carthaginians to accept, according to Polybius. Livy (30.43) says Scipio burned 500 Carthaginian ships at sea in front of Carthage,, and of the deserters handed over the Latins were beheaded and the Romans crucified. The war indemnity, paid in annual instalments of 200 talents, was a perpetual reminder of defeat; when Carthage offered in 191 to pay off the remainder, Rome refused.

The treaty made Carthage a dependent state, and its clauses created the problems that led to the Third Punic War: the clause about Masinissa's ancestral lands, deliberately vague, allowed the Numidian king to encroach on Carthaginian territory for fifty years with Roman support, and the prohibition on war without Roman permission meant that when Carthage finally fought Masinissa in 150, Rome could claim a breach. Spain, with its silver mines, passed to Rome. Historians see the peace as moderate in that Carthage survived as a city-state, but crushing in that it lost its empire, fleet and independence of action. Scipio's terms were criticised by those in Rome who wanted Carthage destroyed, and Africanus was later portrayed as a defender of Carthaginian survival.

scholarship: Scullard, Scipio Africanus (1970)
Lancel, Carthage (1995)
Hoyos, Mastering the West (2015)

set.detail:
In 201-200 envoys from Attalus I and Rhodes, whose fleets had fought Philip V at Chios and Lade, and from Athens came to Rome to complain about Philip's aggression in the Aegean and Asia Minor, and about the alleged pact of the kings with Antiochus III to divide the Ptolemaic empire. The Senate sent envoys to Greece (Gaius Claudius Nero, Marcus Aemilius Lepidus and Publius Sempronius Tuditanus), who issued an ultimatum to Philip's general Nicanor at Athens and later to Philip himself at Abydos: he must not make war on any Greek state and must submit his disputes with Attalus to arbitration.

In 200 the consul Publius Sulpicius Galba proposed to the comitia centuriata a declaration of war against Philip. Livy (31.6-8) says that the assembly rejected the proposal, the people being exhausted after the long war against Hannibal; a tribune, Quintus Baebius, accused the Senate of stirring up one war after another. Galba then called the people together again and, in a speech that Livy reproduces, argued that it was better to fight Philip in Macedonia than to wait for him to invade Italy, as Hannibal had done; the second vote carried the war.

The reasons for the war are among the most debated questions of Roman history. Holleaux thought the Senate feared the pact of the kings and the union of Macedon and the Seleucid empire; Badian and Gruen stressed Roman concern for prestige and the need to respond to Greek appeals; Harris emphasised the aristocracy's appetite for glory and spoils; Eckstein the systemic instability caused by the collapse of Ptolemaic power ('power transition crisis'). Polybius (16.27, 16.34) preserves the text of the ultimatum and the scene at Abydos, where the young envoy Lepidus confronted Philip. The episode also illustrates the role of the popular assembly, which could, in exceptional circumstances, reject the proposals of the governing class, though only temporarily.

scholarship: Holleaux, Rome, la Grèce et les monarchies hellénistiques (1921)
Harris, War and Imperialism in Republican Rome (1979)
Eckstein, Rome Enters the Greek East (2008)
Warrior, The Initiation of the Second Macedonian War (1996)

set.detail:
In June 197 (the Roman calendar dates it to spring), Titus Quinctius Flamininus, with about 26,000 men including Aetolian cavalry and infantry and 20 elephants, and Philip V, with about 25,000 (16,000 phalangites), were marching parallel to each other in Thessaly on either side of a range of hills called the Dog's Heads (Cynoscephalae), near Scotussa, in thick fog. Advance guards met on the ridge, and the fighting escalated as both commanders fed in reinforcements. Polybius (18.18-27), whose account is the most detailed, says that Philip was drawn into battle on terrain unfavourable to the phalanx.

Philip's right wing, which had reached the ridge and formed up, charged downhill and drove back the Roman left. But his left wing was still arriving in marching order when Flamininus attacked it with the elephants and the legions of the right wing, and routed it. An unnamed military tribune then took 20 maniples from the victorious Roman right and attacked the rear of the Macedonian right wing, which could not turn round. The phalangites raised their sarissas in surrender, but the Romans, not understanding the signal, killed many. Philip lost 8,000 killed and 5,000 captured; the Romans about 700.

Polybius used the battle for his famous comparison of the legion and the phalanx (18.28-32): the phalanx was invincible on its own terms, on level ground and in front, but rigid, while the legion's flexibility allowed it to exploit gaps and terrain. Modern historians have accepted this analysis with reservations, noting the importance of luck and leadership. The victory ended the Second Macedonian War. In the peace of 196, Philip abandoned his possessions in Greece and Asia, surrendered his fleet, paid 1,000 talents and handed over his son Demetrius as a hostage. Flamininus' moderation in leaving Philip on the throne, against Aetolian demands, reflected Roman interest in a stable Macedon as a buffer against the Thracians and Celts, and the Aetolians' resentment of their reduced share of the victory led to the war with Antiochus.

scholarship: Hammond, The Campaign and the Battle of Cynoscephalae in 197 BC, JHS 108 (1988)
Walbank, Philip V of Macedon (1940)

set.detail:
After Scipio's departure in 206, Rome's Spanish possessions were governed by privati cum imperio (Lucius Cornelius Lentulus, Lucius Manlius Acidinus, Gnaeus Cornelius Blasio, Lucius Stertinius) until 197, when the number of praetors was raised from four to six so that two could be sent each year to Spain. Gaius Sempronius Tuditanus received Hispania Citerior (the east coast from the Pyrenees to New Carthage and later inland) and Marcus Helvius Hispania Ulterior (the Baetis valley and the south). They were instructed to fix the boundaries between the two provinces.

The decision marked the formal creation of two permanent provinces, although the conquest of Spain would take two more centuries. The two praetors faced an immediate crisis: the great Spanish revolt of 197, in which the Turdetani, the cities of the Baetis valley and the eastern peoples rose, and Sempronius Tuditanus was killed. Rome sent Cato as consul in 195. Revenues came from the silver and iron mines, especially around New Carthage, and from a tribute in kind (stipendium), raised more irregularly than in Sicily. Cato organised the mines, and the governors of the 180s and 170s, notably Tiberius Gracchus, established a more regular system.

Modern historians (Richardson, Hispaniae) see the creation of the two provinces as a decision taken under military pressure, rather than a planned policy of territorial expansion, but it committed Rome to permanent military involvement in the peninsula, which would demand armies every year and cause many of the social problems of the second century: long military service, loss of manpower, and wealth for the commanders. The Spanish provinces were also the scene of serious abuses, leading to the complaints of 171 and the creation of the extortion court in 149. The boundary between the two provinces shifted over time; in the 150s it ran near Castulo and the Sierra Morena.

scholarship: Richardson, Hispaniae: Spain and the Development of Roman Imperialism (1986)
Brennan, The Praetorship in the Roman Republic (2000)

set.detail:
At the Isthmian Games in spring or early summer 196, a herald announced to the crowd assembled in the stadium near Corinth that the Roman Senate and Titus Quinctius Flamininus, having defeated Philip and the Macedonians, declared free, ungarrisoned, untaxed and governed by their own laws the Corinthians, Phocians, Locrians, Euboeans, Achaeans of Phthiotis, Magnesians, Thessalians and Perrhaebians, the peoples who had been under Macedonian rule. Polybius (18.46) and Plutarch describe the crowd's disbelief, the second proclamation, and the shouting so loud that birds flying over the stadium fell dead.

The declaration was a deliberate act of propaganda, aimed both at Greek opinion and at Antiochus III, who was advancing in Thrace and Asia Minor, and it adopted the slogan of 'freedom of the Greeks' used by Hellenistic kings since Antigonus Monophthalmus. Flamininus and the ten commissioners from Rome debated whether to keep garrisons in the 'fetters of Greece' (Acrocorinth, Chalcis and Demetrias); they evacuated them in 194, after the war against Nabis. Coins and statues honoured Flamininus as a saviour; a gold stater with his portrait, struck in Greece, is among the earliest portraits of a living Roman.

Modern historians have long debated the sincerity of the declaration. Some (Badian, Gruen) see it as a genuine policy based on Roman ideas of clientage, in which freedom meant freedom under Roman patronage; others (Harris) as a cynical instrument of domination; Eckstein emphasises the need for a stable Greek system that excluded the great powers. The meaning of 'freedom' became a point of contention: the Aetolians argued that Rome had simply replaced Macedon as master of Greece, and the subsequent decades of Roman arbitration, interference and finally the destruction of Corinth in 146, at the very place of the declaration, give the episode a tragic irony that Polybius felt keenly.

scholarship: Badian, Foreign Clientelae (1958)
Gruen, The Hellenistic World and the Coming of Rome (1984)
Dmitriev, The Greek Slogan of Freedom and Early Roman Politics in Greece (2011)

set.detail:
Between 196 and 192, Antiochus III and Rome conducted a cold war of diplomacy over the status of the Greek cities of Asia Minor (notably Smyrna and Lampsacus, which appealed to Rome) and Antiochus' presence in Thrace. At the conference of Lysimachia (196) and in later negotiations at Rome (193) and Ephesus, the Romans demanded that Antiochus leave Europe and the autonomous cities of Asia; Antiochus replied that Rome had no more right to interfere in Asia than he had in Italy. Hannibal, who had fled Carthage in 195, was at Antiochus' court, which alarmed the Romans.

The Aetolians, embittered after Cynoscephalae, invited Antiochus to free Greece and in 192 seized Demetrias. In autumn 192 Antiochus crossed with only 10,000 infantry, 500 cavalry and six elephants, far too small a force, and landed at Demetrias, where the Aetolians elected him their supreme commander. He took Chalcis and won over Boeotia, Elis and part of Thessaly, but the Achaeans, Philip V and most of the Greeks sided with Rome or stayed neutral. He spent the winter at Chalcis, where he married a young local woman, a symbol, for Polybius and Livy, of his lost momentum.

Rome declared war in 191 and sent the consul Manius Acilius Glabrio with about 20,000 men, along with Philip V's support. The war was decided at Thermopylae in spring 191. Historians debate the war's causes: Badian saw a 'cold war' in which neither side wanted a real war, Gruen a series of misunderstandings, Grainger Antiochus' miscalculation in trusting the Aetolians' promises of Greek support. Antiochus' landing with so few troops suggests that he hoped to negotiate from strength rather than conquer Greece. Hannibal's advice, according to Livy, was to invade Italy with a large force and to secure the alliance of Philip; Antiochus did not follow it.

scholarship: Badian, Rome and Antiochus the Great: A Study in Cold War, CPh 54 (1959)
Grainger, The Roman War of Antiochos the Great (2002)
Ma, Antiochos III and the Cities of Western Asia Minor (1999)

set.detail:
In spring 191 Antiochus III, with about 10,000 men, fortified the pass of Thermopylae against the consul Manius Acilius Glabrio, who had about 20,000 Roman and allied troops plus elephants and Philip V's support. Antiochus built a double rampart and ditch across the narrow pass between the mountains and the sea, placed his light troops on the heights, and asked the Aetolians to hold the mountain paths, including the path of Anopaea used by the Persians in 480, with 4,000 men in the forts of Callidromus, Teichious and Rhoduntia.

Glabrio sent two former consuls serving as military tribunes, Marcus Porcius Cato and Lucius Valerius Flaccus, with 2,000 men each to dislodge the Aetolians at night. Flaccus failed at Teichious and Rhoduntia, but Cato, after a difficult night march guided by a captured Aetolian, surprised and routed the Aetolians at Callidromus at dawn and appeared above the Seleucid camp as Glabrio attacked the front. Antiochus' army, caught between two forces, fled. Antiochus, wounded in the mouth by a stone, escaped with 500 cavalry to Chalcis and sailed to Ephesus. Livy reports that only 500 of his army escaped; the Romans lost 200 men.

Cato's role was decisive, and he made sure that it was known: Plutarch quotes his account, in which Glabrio embraced him before the army and said that neither he nor the Roman people could repay him. The battle ended Antiochus' European venture; he abandoned Greece and returned to Asia, leaving the Aetolians to face Rome alone. The parallel with Leonidas, whose last stand at the same place was outflanked by the same mountain path, was obvious to ancient writers. Glabrio then besieged Heraclea and Naupactus, and the war moved to Asia Minor in 190, where the Scipio brothers led the Roman army. Modern historians (Grainger) regard Antiochus' strategy as defensive and his defeat as the result of excessive reliance on unreliable allies.

scholarship: Grainger, The Roman War of Antiochos the Great (2002)
Astin, Cato the Censor (1978)

set.detail:
In late 190 or early 189 (the Roman calendar date is late 190; in Julian terms perhaps January 189), the Roman army under the consul Lucius Cornelius Scipio, accompanied by his brother Africanus as legate, crossed the Hellespont and met Antiochus III on the plain near Magnesia ad Sipylum, in Lydia. Africanus was ill at Elaea, and the actual command was exercised by the experienced Gnaeus Domitius Ahenobarbus. The Romans had about 30,000 men, including two Roman legions, two allied legions, Eumenes II's cavalry and Achaean light troops; Antiochus, according to Livy, had 60,000 infantry, 12,000 cavalry, 54 elephants and scythed chariots, including cataphracts, Arab camel riders, Galatians and a phalanx of 16,000.

The battle began badly for the Seleucids: Eumenes' archers and slingers panicked the scythed chariots on the Seleucid left, which turned back and disordered their own cavalry and the left flank of the phalanx. Eumenes then charged with his cavalry and routed the Seleucid left. Antiochus, commanding the cataphracts on his right, routed the Roman left and pursued it to the Roman camp, where he was stopped by the camp guard under Marcus Aemilius Lepidus. Meanwhile, the Seleucid phalanx, attacked by Roman missiles and its own panicked elephants, broke. Livy says 50,000 infantry and 3,000 cavalry of Antiochus were killed, 1,400 captured with 15 elephants; the Romans lost 300 infantry and 24 cavalry, and Eumenes 25 men.

The casualty figures are absurd, but the defeat was total. Antiochus sued for peace, accepting the Roman preliminary terms at Sardis, confirmed at Apamea in 188. Lucius Scipio celebrated a triumph and took the cognomen Asiaticus. Magnesia ended the Seleucid challenge to Rome and established Roman hegemony in the eastern Mediterranean. Modern historians emphasise the decisive role of Eumenes and the weaknesses of the Seleucid army, which, despite its size, was composed of disparate contingents, and debate the date, given the discrepancy between the Roman calendar and the solar year shown by the eclipse of 190.

scholarship: Bar-Kochva, The Seleucid Army (1976)
Grainger, The Roman War of Antiochos the Great (2002)

set.detail:
After Magnesia, Antiochus' envoys accepted the Roman terms at Sardis in early 189, and the final treaty was drawn up by the proconsul Gnaeus Manlius Vulso and ten commissioners at Apamea in Phrygia in 188. Polybius (21.42-45) and Livy (38.38) give the terms: Antiochus gave up all territory west of the Taurus mountains and north of the river Halys; he surrendered all his elephants and could keep no more; his navy was limited to ten decked ships, which could not sail west of Cape Sarpedon in Cilicia except to carry tribute, envoys or hostages; he was not to recruit mercenaries or receive fugitives from Roman territory; he paid 15,000 Euboean talents, 500 immediately, 2,500 on ratification, and 12,000 over twelve years; he handed over 20 hostages, including his son Antiochus (the future Antiochus IV), and Hannibal, the Aetolian Thoas and other enemies of Rome.

The territory surrendered was distributed among Rome's allies: Eumenes II received most of Asia Minor west of the Taurus, including Lydia, Phrygia, Lycaonia and the Thracian Chersonese, making Pergamon a major power; Rhodes received Lycia and Caria south of the Maeander. The Greek cities that had supported Rome were declared free; those that had supported Antiochus were given to Eumenes or Rhodes. Hannibal escaped to Crete and then Bithynia. The treaty's terms on the navy and elephants were later enforced brutally by Gnaeus Octavius in 162.

The indemnity, the largest in ancient history, and the territorial losses crippled the Seleucid state: Antiochus III died in 187 trying to plunder a temple in Elymais to pay it. Rome took no territory for itself, preferring to strengthen its allies, a policy that historians have described as hegemony without annexation. The treaty marked the high point of Pergamene and Rhodian power, both later reduced by Rome after the Third Macedonian War. Modern historians debate whether Rome deliberately sought to weaken the Seleucids permanently, or was simply establishing a balance of power in its favour in the Hellenistic world.

scholarship: McDonald, The Treaty of Apamea, JRS 57 (1967)
Gruen, The Hellenistic World and the Coming of Rome (1984)
Grainger, The Roman War of Antiochos the Great (2002)

set.detail:
The trials of the Scipios are among the most confused episodes in Roman history, because Livy (38.50-60) reports several conflicting versions, drawn from Valerius Antias, Claudius Quadrigarius and others, and admits he cannot decide between them. The core is clear: in 187, at the instigation of Cato, the tribunes Quintus Petillius and Quintus Petillius Spurinus demanded that Lucius Scipio Asiaticus account for 500 talents received from Antiochus III as the first instalment of the indemnity, or as money for the army's pay. Africanus, who had served as his brother's legate, produced the account books in the Senate and tore them up, saying it was unworthy to have to account for 500 talents when he had brought 15,000 into the treasury.

Lucius was condemned to a fine, and when he refused to give sureties, the tribune ordered him to prison; another tribune, Tiberius Sempronius Gracchus, father of the Gracchi and a personal enemy of the Scipios, vetoed the imprisonment out of respect for the family's dignity. According to tradition, Gracchus was then betrothed to Africanus' daughter Cornelia. Lucius' property was sold, and it turned out to be insufficient to pay the fine, which some saw as proof of his innocence. Africanus himself was accused, perhaps in 184, by the tribune Marcus Naevius; on the day of the trial, the anniversary of Zama, he reminded the people of his victory and led them to the Capitol to give thanks to the gods, leaving the tribune alone. He then retired to his villa at Liternum, where he died in 183.

Modern historians (Scullard, Gruen, Astin) have tried to reconstruct the sequence, generally accepting that the attacks were part of a political campaign led by Cato and his allies against the dominant position of the Scipios after the Antiochus war, and against the increasing wealth and independence of the great generals. The trials marked the end of Africanus' political dominance and demonstrated the limits that the Roman aristocracy placed on individual pre-eminence. The many variants also show how Roman historical memory shaped the story of the 'ungrateful Republic'.

scholarship: Scullard, Roman Politics 220-150 BC (1951)
Gruen, The Fall of the Scipios, in Leaders and Masses in the Roman World (1995)
Astin, Cato the Censor (1978)

set.detail:
In 186 the consul Spurius Postumius Albinus learned from the freedwoman Hispala Faecenia, lover of the young Publius Aebutius, that Aebutius' mother and stepfather planned to initiate him into the Bacchic rites to get rid of him. Hispala, who had been initiated as a slave, described the rites: originally held three times a year for women only in daytime, they had been reformed by a Campanian priestess, Paculla Annia, who admitted men and held them at night five times a month; there was drunkenness, sexual excess, forgery, poisoning and murder. Postumius reported to the Senate, which ordered an inquiry throughout Italy.

Livy (39.8-19) describes a panic in Rome: 7,000 men and women were reportedly involved, many fled, and many were executed; women were handed over to their families for execution. The Senate's decree, known from a bronze tablet found at Tiriolo in Bruttium in 1640 (CIL I2 581, the senatus consultum de Bacchanalibus, now in Vienna), shows the measures. Bacchic groups were not banned outright, but placed under strict control: no man could be a priest; groups could have no common funds, officials or oaths; meetings had to be authorised by the urban praetor and the Senate, with no more than five people (two men and three women) present.

Modern historians have interpreted the affair in many ways: as a moral panic about a foreign cult (Gruen), as an assertion of Roman authority over Italian religion and communities (North), as a reaction against private associations independent of the state, or as a political attack by the Senate on the Campanian and southern Italian elites. The decree's application to the allies, who were formally independent, illustrates the growing interference of Rome in Italian affairs after the Hannibalic war. The cult of Bacchus was not suppressed: Bacchic imagery remained common, and Caesar is said to have restored the rites. The tablet of Tiriolo, in archaic Latin, is one of the most important Latin inscriptions of the Republic.

scholarship: North, Religious Toleration in Republican Rome, PCPhS 25 (1979)
Gruen, Studies in Greek Culture and Roman Policy (1990)
Pailler, Bacchanalia (1988)

set.detail:
In 184 Marcus Porcius Cato and his friend Lucius Valerius Flaccus were elected censors after a bitter campaign against seven other candidates, including Lucius Scipio Asiaticus and Lucius Valerius Tappo, on a platform promising severe reform. Cato's censorship became legendary for its severity. He expelled seven senators from the Senate, including Lucius Quinctius Flamininus, consul 192 and brother of Titus, for killing a Gallic deserter (or a condemned prisoner) at dinner to please a favourite, and Manilius, who was expelled for kissing his wife in daylight in front of their daughter. He deprived Lucius Scipio of his public horse.

Cato and Flaccus imposed heavy taxes on luxury goods: jewellery, women's clothing and carriages worth more than 15,000 asses were assessed at ten times their value and taxed at three per thousand; expensive slaves bought recently were similarly assessed. They cut off public water that private individuals had diverted to their houses and gardens, and demolished buildings that encroached on public land. They let public contracts at the highest rents and lowest prices, which led to protests from the publicani; the Senate cancelled the contracts and ordered new ones, which were only slightly less strict.

Cato also built the Basilica Porcia next to the Curia, the first basilica in Rome, and reconstructed the city's sewers. Flaccus was chosen princeps senatus. Cato's censorship became a symbol of austerity and the Roman resistance to Hellenistic luxury, and gave him his traditional cognomen Censorius. Plutarch says the people set up a statue of him in the temple of Health with an inscription praising him for restoring the Republic through good guidance and sound principles. Modern historians (Astin) stress that Cato's measures, although harsh, were directed at the political and economic consequences of the eastern wars, especially the concentration of wealth among the elite, and that his attacks on rivals, such as the Flaminini and Scipios, were part of aristocratic competition. His speeches as censor, preserved in fragments, show his rhetorical force.

scholarship: Astin, Cato the Censor (1978)
Suolahti, The Roman Censors (1963)

set.detail:
After the battle of Magnesia, the treaty of Apamea required the surrender of Hannibal. He fled, first to Crete, where Nepos tells how he deceived the Gortynians by filling amphorae with lead and leaving them in the temple of Artemis while hiding his gold in hollow bronze statues, and then perhaps to Armenia, where Strabo and Plutarch say he advised King Artaxias on the founding of Artaxata. Eventually he took refuge with Prusias I of Bithynia, for whom he commanded a fleet against Eumenes II and won a naval victory using jars of snakes.

In 183 Titus Quinctius Flamininus, as Roman envoy to Prusias, demanded Hannibal's surrender (whether on the Senate's orders or on his own initiative is disputed). Prusias' soldiers surrounded Hannibal's house at Libyssa, on the Gulf of Nicomedia. Finding all exits guarded, Hannibal took poison that he kept in a ring, saying, according to Livy (39.51), 'let us free the Roman people from their long anxiety, since they think it too long to wait for the death of an old man'. He was about 64. Livy also mentions the year of his death as 183, the same as that of Scipio Africanus and Philopoemen, though other authors place it in 182 or 181.

Hannibal's tomb at Libyssa was still shown in Pliny's time; the emperor Septimius Severus, an African, is said to have covered it with white marble. Flamininus was criticised in Rome for hounding an old man to death. Polybius (23.13) concludes his portrait of Hannibal by praising his ability to hold together an army of many different nations for sixteen years without mutiny. Hannibal remained the greatest enemy in Roman memory; Juvenal mocked the futility of his ambition that ended in a ring. Modern biographers (Lancel, Hoyos, Seibert) debate his strategic choices, particularly his failure to march on Rome after Cannae, and his political role in Carthage after the war.

scholarship: Lancel, Hannibal (1998)
Hoyos, Hannibal: Rome's Greatest Enemy (2008)
Seibert, Hannibal (1993)

set.detail:
In 180 the tribune Lucius Villius carried a law that, according to Livy (40.44), established the minimum ages for each magistracy; his family was later known as Annales for this reason. The precise provisions are not recorded, but they can be reconstructed from the careers of subsequent politicians: a minimum age of about 30 for the quaestorship (after ten years of military service), 36 or 37 for the aedileship, 39 or 40 for the praetorship and 42 or 43 for the consulship. The law probably also required a two-year interval (biennium) between curule offices, and made the praetorship a mandatory step before the consulship.

The law codified the cursus honorum, the established order of offices, which had been taking shape in the early second century. Before 180, young men like Scipio Africanus (aedile at about 22, consul at 31) and Flamininus (consul at about 29) could reach the highest offices quickly in exceptional circumstances. The law responded to the intensification of aristocratic competition and the risk of exceptional careers: it gave more men an opportunity to reach the consulship and limited the advantage of the great families. The lex Baebia of 181 on the number of praetors and the laws on ambitus of 181 and 159 were part of the same effort to regulate competition.

The law was not always respected: Scipio Aemilianus was elected consul in 147 at about 37, before the legal age, by a special dispensation, and again in 134, in violation of the prohibition on second consulships (c. 151). Sulla's lex Cornelia de magistratibus (81) reaffirmed and modified the rules. Modern historians (Astin, Evans and Kleijwegt) have debated the precise ages, using the careers of known politicians, and the motivations for the law, seeing it as an indication of the oligarchy's efforts to maintain equality among its members and to prevent the rise of a dominant individual, as seen with Africanus.

scholarship: Astin, The Lex Annalis before Sulla, Latomus 16-17 (1957-1958)
Evans and Kleijwegt, Did the Romans Like Young Men?, ZPE 92 (1992)
Beck, Karriere und Hierarchie (2005)

set.detail:
After three years of indecisive campaigns, Lucius Aemilius Paullus, consul for the second time at about 60, took command in Macedonia in 168, restored discipline, outflanked Perseus' line on the Elpeus via Pythium thanks to Scipio Nasica's march, and forced him back to the plain near Pydna. On the night before the battle, the military tribune Gaius Sulpicius Galus predicted a lunar eclipse, which took place on 21 June 168 (Julian; Livy's date, 3/4 September, reflects the Roman calendar error), and the Macedonians were frightened by it. The battle began the next afternoon, apparently by accident, after a skirmish over a horse that had escaped near the river.

Perseus had about 44,000 men, including 21,000 phalangites; Paullus about 38,000, including two Roman legions and allied troops and 22 elephants. The Macedonian phalanx charged, and Paullus later said that he had never seen anything so terrifying as the advancing wall of sarissas. The Paelignian cohort and the first legion were pushed back. But as the phalanx advanced over uneven ground, gaps opened in its ranks, and Paullus ordered his maniples to penetrate these gaps and attack the phalangites from the sides, where their long spears were useless. The elephants and allied infantry routed the Macedonian left. The 3,000 elite peltasts, the agema, fought to the death. In about an hour the battle was over.

Plutarch and Livy say 20,000 Macedonians were killed and 11,000 captured; the Romans lost about 100. Perseus fled to Pella and then to Samothrace, where he surrendered. The battle ended the Antigonid monarchy, which had ruled Macedonia since 277. Polybius, who knew the participants, gave the main account, used by Livy and Plutarch. Paullus' victory monument at Delphi, a pillar originally intended for a statue of Perseus, survives with a frieze showing the battle, including the escaped horse. Modern historians see Pydna as confirmation of Polybius' analysis of the superiority of the legion over the phalanx, but stress the role of leadership and terrain.

scholarship: Hammond, The Battle of Pydna, JHS 104 (1984)
Kähler, Der Fries vom Reiterdenkmal des Aemilius Paullus in Delphi (1965)
Taylor, The Battle Scene on Aemilius Paullus's Pydna Monument: A Reevaluation, Hesperia 85 (2016)

set.detail:
In 168 Antiochus IV invaded Egypt for the second time, after the reconciliation of Ptolemy VI and Ptolemy VIII, occupied Memphis, sent a fleet to Cyprus, and advanced on Alexandria. At Eleusis, a suburb about six kilometres east of Alexandria, he was met by a Roman embassy led by Gaius Popillius Laenas, consul 172, which had waited at Delos until news of the Roman victory at Pydna arrived. Popillius handed Antiochus the Senate's decree ordering him to leave Egypt and Cyprus immediately. When Antiochus said he wanted to consult his advisers, Popillius drew a circle in the sand around the king with a vine stick and told him to give his answer before leaving the circle.

Antiochus, after a moment's hesitation, agreed to comply, and Popillius then gave him his hand as a friend. Polybius (29.27), who tells the story, explains that Antiochus yielded because he knew of the Roman victory at Pydna and did not want to risk war with Rome. He withdrew his army from Egypt within the time prescribed, and his fleet from Cyprus, bitterly resentful. The episode is the classic example of Roman hegemony exercised by diplomacy, based on the prestige of recent victories, without the use of force.

The 'Day of Eleusis' saved the Ptolemaic kingdom, which became dependent on Roman protection. Its consequences extended beyond Egypt: according to the Book of Daniel (11.30, 'ships of Kittim shall come against him'), Antiochus, frustrated in Egypt, took out his anger on Jerusalem, where he imposed the measures that triggered the Maccabean revolt. He then held the great festival at Daphne in 166 to restore his prestige. Modern historians (Gruen, Morgan) have discussed whether the Senate intended to take control of Egypt or simply to prevent a Seleucid takeover, and whether Polybius' account, which emphasises Roman superiority, is literally accurate. The phrase 'to draw a line in the sand' has been associated with this event.

scholarship: Morgan, The Perils of Schematism: Polybius, Antiochus Epiphanes and the Day of Eleusis, Historia 39 (1990)
Gruen, Rome and the Seleucids in the Aftermath of Pydna, Chiron 6 (1976)

set.detail:
In November 167 Lucius Aemilius Paullus celebrated a three-day triumph over Perseus and Macedonia, described in detail by Plutarch (Aemilius 32-34) and Livy (45.40). On the first day 250 wagons carried statues and paintings; on the second, the finest Macedonian weapons and armour, followed by 3,000 men carrying silver coins in 750 vessels each containing three talents, and silver bowls, horns and cups. On the third day, 120 oxen for sacrifice, gold coins in 77 vessels, a sacred gold bowl weighing ten talents, the gold plate of Perseus, his chariot, armour and diadem. Then came the king's children with their attendants, and Perseus himself, dressed in black, followed by his friends. Then Paullus himself, in a gilded chariot and purple robe. Livy says that the money brought to the treasury amounted to 120 million sesterces (or 300 million in another version).

Before the triumph, the soldiers, encouraged by Servius Sulpicius Galba, opposed the triumph because Paullus had given them too little booty; it was saved by the speech of the elderly consular Marcus Servilius. Plutarch tells the tragic story of Paullus' two younger sons, who died during the triumph, one five days before and the other three days after; the other two had been adopted into the families of the Fabii and the Scipios. In his speech to the people, Paullus said that he had prayed that if Fortune envied Rome's success, she would turn her anger on him and his house rather than on the state, and that his prayer had been answered.

The triumph marked a turning point in Roman finances: the booty was so large that the tributum, the direct tax on Roman citizens, was suspended indefinitely. Paullus gave Perseus' library to his sons Scipio Aemilianus and Fabius, the start of the Scipionic interest in Greek culture. Perseus was imprisoned at Alba Fucens, where he died a few years later. The triumph is one of the best documented of the Republic and has served as a model for studies of the ceremony (Beard, The Roman Triumph).

scholarship: Beard, The Roman Triumph (2007)
Östenberg, Staging the World (2009)

set.detail:
In 167, at Amphipolis, Lucius Aemilius Paullus and ten senatorial commissioners announced the settlement of Macedonia. The monarchy was abolished. Macedonia was declared free, but divided into four separate republics (merides), with capitals at Amphipolis, Thessalonica, Pella and Pelagonia. Each had its own council (synedrion) and magistrates. The Macedonians would pay Rome half the tribute they had paid the king, 100 talents a year. Marriage (conubium) and the acquisition of land (commercium) between citizens of different republics were prohibited.

The royal gold and silver mines were closed (only copper and iron mines remained open) to prevent them from being exploited by publicani or financing a revolt; the royal forests, which supplied timber for shipbuilding, were also closed and the import of salt restricted. The four republics, except those bordering the barbarians, were forbidden to maintain armies. The leading men of the old monarchy, the king's friends and officers and their sons over 15, were deported to Italy. Paullus then held great games at Amphipolis, which Polybius describes as a model of organisation, and drafted a constitution for the Macedonians, which Livy says lasted a long time.

The settlement shows Roman reluctance to annex territory directly in the East at that time; the four republics, with their restrictions, were designed to prevent the rise of a new monarchy. But the arrangement was unstable: the four republics were economically weakened, the mines were reopened in 158, and in 149 the pretender Andriscus, claiming to be the son of Perseus, easily reunited Macedonia. After his defeat in 148, Macedonia became a Roman province in 146. Silver tetradrachms of the merides, especially the First (Amphipolis) with Artemis on a Macedonian shield, are common in hoards and show the economic activity of the republics after 158. Modern historians (Gruen, Hammond) debate whether Rome intended to weaken Macedonia permanently or to establish free republics on the Greek model.

scholarship: Gruen, Macedonia and the Settlement of 167 BC, in Philip II, Alexander the Great and the Macedonian Heritage (1982)
Hammond and Walbank, A History of Macedonia III (1988)

set.detail:
During the Third Macedonian War, the Molossians of Epirus, under Cephalus and Theodotus, had joined Perseus, while other Epirote peoples remained loyal to Rome. In 167 the Senate ordered Aemilius Paullus to punish the Epirote cities that had defected and to give their plunder to his soldiers. Paullus sent centurions to the 70 towns of the Molossians, announcing that the Roman garrisons would be withdrawn and asking the towns to collect their gold and silver; then, on a pre-arranged day, his soldiers simultaneously plundered all the towns. According to Polybius (30.15), followed by Livy (45.34) and Plutarch, 150,000 people were sold into slavery and the walls of the towns were demolished.

The booty, Livy says, was so great that each infantryman received 200 denarii and each cavalryman 400, yet even this sum was criticised as meagre by the soldiers. Strabo, writing two centuries later, says that Epirus was still depopulated in his time, with the villages of the Molossians deserted. The episode was one of the most brutal acts of Roman warfare of the period, comparable to the massacres in Spain and the destruction of Carthage and Corinth twenty years later.

Modern historians have seen the sack of Epirus as an example of the Senate's use of terror to deter defection, and as evidence of the economic motive of Roman warfare: the massive supply of slaves fed the expanding villa economy of Italy. The figure of 150,000 has been questioned, since it would represent almost the entire population of Molossia, but most accept that the number was very large. The sack contrasts sharply with Paullus' reputation for personal integrity and his philhellenism, illustrating the coexistence of cultural admiration and military brutality in Roman attitudes towards the Greeks. It also shows the Senate's willingness to reward its armies at the expense of provincials, a practice that would contribute to the development of professional armies loyal to their commanders.

scholarship: Hammond, Epirus (1967)
Ziolkowski, Urbs direpta, or How the Romans Sacked Cities, in War and Society in the Roman World (1993)

set.detail:
After Pydna, Roman commissioners went to Greece to investigate the conduct of Greek politicians during the war. In Achaea, the pro-Roman politician Callicrates gave them a list of about 1,000 Achaeans who, he claimed, had favoured Perseus or had not supported Rome enough. They were deported to Italy for trial, although no trial was ever held, and were dispersed among the towns of Etruria. Among them was Polybius, son of Lycortas, who had been hipparchus of the Achaean League in 170/169.

Polybius, thanks to his friendship with Scipio Aemilianus and Fabius Maximus Aemilianus, the sons of Aemilius Paullus, was allowed to stay in Rome, where he became Scipio's mentor and friend, as he describes (31.23-30). This situation gave him access to the Roman political elite and to documents, and inspired him to write his history of the rise of Rome to world power in 53 years. The other hostages remained in Etruria; Achaean embassies repeatedly asked for their release, but the Senate refused, in part because of Callicrates' influence.

In 150, after 17 years, the Senate released the 300 survivors, after Scipio Aemilianus intervened and Cato made his famous remark about Greek old men. The returning exiles, embittered, became leaders of the anti-Roman party in the Achaean League, contributing to the Achaean War of 146. Pausanias (7.10) describes how Callicrates, called a traitor, was hated so much that the Achaeans would not bathe in the same baths as him. The deportation illustrates Rome's methods of control in Greece after 168: reliance on loyal local elites and removal of potential opponents. For historians, its main consequence was the work of Polybius, without which Roman history of the third and second centuries would be much less well known.

scholarship: Walbank, Polybius (1972)
Champion, Cultural Politics in Polybius's Histories (2004)

set.detail:
The tributum was a direct tax on the property of Roman citizens, levied according to census class to pay for the army, traditionally since the siege of Veii (c. 406). It was not a regular annual tax but was imposed by the Senate according to need, at a rate of usually one per thousand of assessed property (sometimes more in emergencies), and it could be refunded from booty if a war was profitable, as happened after some campaigns.

In 167, after the triumph of Aemilius Paullus, which brought to the treasury, according to Pliny and Plutarch, 300 million sesterces (Livy 120 million), the tributum was no longer collected. Pliny (33.56), Cicero (Off. 2.76) and Plutarch say that Paullus brought so much money from Macedonia that the people ceased to pay the tax. Revenue from the provinces, from the indemnities paid by Carthage and Antiochus, from the Macedonian tribute and mines, and from the Spanish silver mines, was enough to finance the state.

The tributum was not formally abolished but simply not levied again until the crisis of 43, during the civil wars after the death of Caesar. Its suspension had important consequences: the cost of empire was borne by the provincials and conquered peoples, not by Roman citizens; the relationship between military service and taxation was broken; and Roman citizens in Italy enjoyed a significant privilege, which made citizenship more attractive to the Italian allies, who continued to pay for their own contingents. The end of the tributum is often seen as a symbol of the profitability of Roman imperialism in the second century. Modern historians (Nicolet, Rosenstein) debate whether the end of the tributum reflected a deliberate policy or simply a fiscal surplus, and its effects on the relationship between the Roman state and its citizens.

scholarship: Nicolet, Tributum (1976)
Rosenstein, Rome and the Mediterranean 290 to 146 BC (2012)
Tan, Power and Public Finance at Rome (2017)

set.detail:
In 155 Athens, fined 500 talents by a Sicyonian arbitration for raiding the town of Oropus, sent three heads of philosophical schools to Rome to ask for a reduction of the fine: Carneades of Cyrene, head of the Academy; Diogenes of Babylon, head of the Stoa; and Critolaus of Phaselis, head of the Peripatos. The senator Gaius Acilius acted as their interpreter before the Senate, which reduced the fine to 100 talents.

While waiting, the philosophers gave public lectures that attracted huge crowds of young Romans. Carneades, a master of the sceptical method of arguing both sides of a question, spoke one day in praise of justice and the next day against it, arguing that if the Romans were just they would have to give back their empire and return to their huts. Cato, then 79, alarmed at the effect on Roman youth, urged the Senate to settle the business quickly and send the philosophers home, so that young Romans could listen to the laws and magistrates as before, according to Plutarch (Cato 22).

The embassy is considered a landmark in the introduction of Greek philosophy to Rome. It followed the expulsion of Epicureans in 173 and of philosophers and rhetoricians by senatus consultum in 161, and preceded the integration of Greek philosophy into Roman aristocratic culture with Panaetius and Scipio Aemilianus. Cicero (Republic 3) used Carneades' speech against justice as the basis for the argument of Furius Philus. Modern historians (Gruen, Powell) see the episode as reflecting the ambivalence of Roman attitudes to Greek culture: admiration, curiosity and a sense of threat to traditional values. Cato's opposition was not total rejection of Greek culture, since he himself learned Greek; it was an assertion that Roman values must have priority.

scholarship: Gruen, Culture and National Identity in Republican Rome (1992)
Powell, The Embassy of the Three Philosophers to Rome in 155 BC, in Kremmydas and Tempest (eds.), Hellenistic Oratory (2013)

set.detail:
In 153 (some say 152), Cato served on a senatorial embassy sent to arbitrate a border dispute between Carthage and Masinissa. He was struck by the prosperity of Carthage: its fertile land, large population, abundant arms and supplies. According to Plutarch (Cato 26-27), he returned to Rome convinced that Carthage was a mortal danger, and, showing the Senate a fresh fig from Carthage, he said that the place where such fruit grew was only three days' sail from Rome. From then on he ended every speech in the Senate, whatever the subject, with the words 'ceterum censeo Carthaginem esse delendam' ('moreover, I think Carthage must be destroyed').

The exact formula 'Carthago delenda est' is a modern reworking; the ancient sources give variants, the earliest in Plutarch in Greek. Scipio Nasica Corculum opposed Cato, ending his speeches with the opposite sentiment, that Carthage should be preserved; he argued that fear of Carthage was necessary to maintain Roman discipline and unity (metus Punicus), an argument later developed by Sallust and Diodorus (via Posidonius) as an explanation for Roman moral decline after 146.

Modern historians have debated whether Carthage was really a danger to Rome in the 150s. Archaeology has confirmed Carthage's prosperity in this period: new residential quarters on the Byrsa hill (the 'Hannibal quarter') and the circular military harbour. Some (Harris) see Cato's campaign as a manifestation of Roman aggressiveness; others (Astin) argue that Cato genuinely feared Carthaginian revival, especially after Carthage built up its forces against Masinissa; still others see economic motives (competition in agricultural exports, such as wine and oil), although this is disputed. The Senate's decision for war in 150-149 was influenced by Cato's campaign, Masinissa's encroachments and Carthage's violation of the treaty of 201.

scholarship: Astin, Cato the Censor (1978)
Harris, War and Imperialism in Republican Rome (1979)
Little, The Origin of the Third Punic War, CPh 29 (1934)

set.detail:
In 151-150, the Lusitanians, who had raided Roman territory in Hispania Ulterior since 155, were attacked by the praetor Servius Sulpicius Galba, who had already suffered a defeat in 151, and by Lucius Licinius Lucullus, who had moved into Lusitania from Citerior after his massacre at Cauca. In 150 the Lusitanians sent envoys to Galba offering to renew the treaty made with the praetor Atilius in 152. Galba, according to Appian (Iberica 59-60), pretended to sympathise with their poverty, which forced them to raid, and promised to give them good land if they laid down their arms.

He divided the Lusitanians into three groups, settled them in three places, and told them to wait for him; then he went to each group in turn, ordered them to lay down their arms, surrounded them with a ditch, and had them massacred. Appian says that few escaped; Valerius Maximus and Orosius give figures of 8,000 killed or 30,000 Lusitanians killed and enslaved. Galba distributed little of the booty to his soldiers and kept most for himself. Among the survivors was Viriathus, who became the great leader of the Lusitanian resistance in the following years.

In 149 the tribune Lucius Scribonius Libo proposed a law to create a special court to try Galba, supported by Cato in one of his last speeches. Galba escaped condemnation by appealing to the pity of the people, presenting his young children and his orphaned ward. The failure of the prosecution led to the creation of the permanent court for the recovery of money extorted by governors, under the lex Calpurnia of 149. Galba became consul in 144 and was regarded by Cicero as one of the greatest orators of his time. Modern historians see the massacre as a symptom of the violence of Roman warfare in Spain and of the impunity of Roman commanders, and as the immediate cause of the long Lusitanian War.

scholarship: Richardson, Hispaniae (1986)
Simon, Roms Kriege in Spanien 154-133 v. Chr. (1962)
